examples.solution_text:
A: All five columns have the same height. There is no peak, so the distribution is uniform.

B: The frequencies rise towards scores $3$ and $4$, then fall. These adjacent equally tall columns form one flat-topped peak because there is no dip between them. The distribution is unimodal.

The stacks at $2$ and $6$ books are taller than their neighbours, with shorter stacks between them. There are two separate peaks, so the distribution is bimodal. The peaks do not need to have equal heights.

examples.question_text:
The frequency table shows the number of minutes students spent travelling to school. Describe the modality of the distribution.

$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Travel time (minutes)}&\text{Frequency}\\\hline 0\text{–}9&2\\10\text{–}19&8\\20\text{–}29&3\\30\text{–}39&1\\40\text{–}49&6\\50\text{–}59&2\end{array}$
examples.solution_text:
The frequencies rise from $2$ to $8$, fall through $3$ to $1$, then rise to $6$ before falling to $2$.

The groups $10\text{–}19$ and $40\text{–}49$ minutes form two peaks separated by lower frequencies. The distribution is bimodal.

The curve has three high regions separated by dips. It has three peaks, so the distribution is multimodal.

Modality counts peaks rather than their heights. The different heights do not change the classification.

a. B has one peak, so it is unimodal.

b. A has two peaks separated by a dip, so it is bimodal.

c. C has three peaks separated by dips, so it is multimodal.

examples.derivation: A has frequencies 4,4,4,4,4: a flat display with no peak, hence uniform. B has frequencies 1,3,5,5,2: the adjacent equal maxima form one high region without an intervening dip, hence unimodal. This follows the supplied peak-counting convention.

The dot-stack frequencies are 1,5,2,1,2,4,1. Values 2 and 6 each exceed their neighbours, and shorter stacks separate them. There are two unequal peaks, hence bimodal, consistent with the source's definition.

The ordered frequencies 2,8,3,1,6,2 have local maxima at 10–19 and 40–49 minutes, separated by lower frequencies. The distribution is bimodal. This applies the source's peak-counting definition to its supported ordered frequency-table representation.

The authored Bézier curve rises and falls through three maxima at heights 3.3,2.1,2.8, with intervening minima at 0.7 and 0.5. Each segment is monotonic between these extrema. Three separate peaks give a multimodal distribution; unequal heights do not change the count.

Curve A has two maxima separated by one dip; B has one maximum; C has three maxima separated by two dips. The matches are a: B, b: A, c: C. The Bézier paths agree with these counts and use the source's description-to-display matching method.
